steps.title: Import React from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React from the 'react' package to enable JSX syntax and React component functionality.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React into your file. This is required for writing JSX.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React
import React from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library is imported, allowing you to use JSX and React features in your component.
successCriteria: Import statement present
Imports React from 'react'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React. This is the foundation for writing React components with JSX.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing React specifically from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import React from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Create main component function
steps.instruction: Create a function component named App that returns JSX.Element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component function that returns JSX. For TypeScript, you can specify the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.seedCode:
import React from 'react';

// Create your App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a functional component named App that returns JSX.Element.
successCriteria: The code must include a component named App that is a function (declaration or arrow) and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your App component returns JSX.Element and has the correct name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component is missing or doesn't meet the requirements. Check that you've created a function named App that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize a state variable
steps.instruction: Import the useState hook from 'react' and declare a state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create state. Remember to import it from 'react' and call it inside your component.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useState hook is imported and a state variable 'isActive' is declared with an initial value of false.
successCriteria: 1. Import useState from 'react'. 2. Declare a state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false using useState. 3. The state declaration should be inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported useState and initialized the isActive state variable. This will allow us to dynamically change styles based on state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there's something missing. Make sure you've: 1) Imported useState from 'react', 2) Declared the state variable inside the App component, and 3) Named it 'isActive' with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Remember to: 1) Import useState from 'react', 2) Declare the state variable inside the App component using useState, and 3) Name it 'isActive' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Create a handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'toggleVisibility' inside your App component that calls the state setter function to toggle the boolean state value.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses the setter function from useState to update the state to the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A toggleVisibility function is defined inside the App component that toggles the boolean state value when called.
successCriteria: Function named 'toggleVisibility' is defined inside App component
Function calls the state setter function
Function toggles the boolean value (e.g., using !prev or !currentValue)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a toggleVisibility function that will toggle your boolean state when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your toggleVisibility function properly toggles the boolean value using the state setter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleVisibility function isn't quite right. Remember to define it inside the App component and have it toggle the boolean state value using the setter function.

steps.title: Return a container div
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, return a <div> element that will serve as the main container for your content.
steps.hint: The return statement should output a JSX <div> element. This will be the root element of your component's UI.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a <div> element containing the existing <h1> heading.
successCriteria: The return statement outputs a JSX <div> element that wraps the existing <h1>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've returned a container <div> element. This provides a structural wrapper for your component's content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your component returns a JSX <div> element that contains the <h1> heading.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't return a <div> element. Check that your return statement outputs JSX with a <div> wrapper.

steps.title: Add a heading with inline styles
steps.instruction: Add an h1 element with inline styles using the style attribute. The style should be a JavaScript object with properties like color, fontSize, and fontWeight.
steps.hint: Use the style attribute on an h1 element. The value should be an object like {{ color: 'blue', fontSize: '2rem' }}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of inline styles on a heading

Styled Heading
steps.expectedOutcome: The h1 element should have inline styles applied via the style attribute with a JavaScript object containing CSS properties.
successCriteria: h1 element exists
style attribute is present
style value is a JavaScript object
object contains at least one CSS property
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added an h1 element with inline styles using a JavaScript object. This demonstrates how to apply styles directly in JSX.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the style attribute with a JavaScript object containing CSS properties like color or fontSize.
steps.feedbackWrong: The h1 element with inline styles wasn't added correctly. Remember to use the style attribute with a JavaScript object containing CSS properties.

steps.instruction:
Inside your component's return statement, add a paragraph element (

steps.hint:
Add a

element inside the container div. Use the style attribute with an object containing CSS properties in camelCase.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a paragraph with inline styles

This is a styled paragraph
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element with custom inline styles appears below the heading in the rendered component.
successCriteria:
Contains a

element
Has text content
Has a style attribute with an object
Object contains at least two CSS properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph with inline styles. Notice how the style object allows you to apply multiple CSS properties directly to the element.
steps.feedbackPartial:

steps.feedbackWrong:

steps.title: Create a styled button
steps.instruction: Add a button element with inline styles to your component. The button should have a background color, text color, padding, and border radius.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element inside the container <div>. Use the style attribute to apply inline styles like backgroundColor, color, padding, and borderRadius.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a styled button
<button style={{ backgroundColor: 'blue', color: 'white', padding: '10px 20px', borderRadius: '5px' }}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element with inline styles appears in the component output.
successCriteria: Button element present
Inline styles applied via style attribute
At least backgroundColor and color styles defined
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button with inline styles. The button now has visual styling applied directly through the style attribute.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but it needs inline styles. Make sure to include a style attribute with at least backgroundColor and color properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element with inline styles is missing. Add a <button> element with a style attribute containing CSS properties like backgroundColor and color.

steps.title: Wire button click to handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick attribute to the button element that calls your toggleVisibility handler function.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on the button element and set it equal to your handler function name without parentheses.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button click to a handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will have an onClick attribute that references the toggleVisibility handler function.
successCriteria: onClick attribute added to button
onClick calls toggleVisibility function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the button's click event to your handler function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the onClick attribute to the button and it references your toggleVisibility function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs an onClick attribute that calls the toggleVisibility handler function.

steps.title: Add a div with dynamic styles
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a <div> element with inline styles that change based on your state variable. The styles should be applied directly to the element using the style attribute with a JavaScript object.
steps.hint: Use the style attribute with an object that contains CSS properties. You can make some properties depend on your state variable using conditional logic.
steps.expectedOutcome: A div element with inline styles that use your state variable to dynamically change appearance.
successCriteria: The code should contain a <div> element with a style attribute that uses an object containing CSS properties. At least one CSS property value should depend on the state variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a div with dynamic inline styles. The styles will update automatically when your state changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a div, but the styles might not be fully dynamic. Make sure at least one CSS property value depends on your state variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The div with dynamic styles wasn't added correctly. Remember to use the style attribute with an object containing CSS properties, and make at least one property value depend on your state variable.

steps.title: Add a styled list
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add an unordered list (<ul>) with three list items (<li>). Apply inline styles to each list item to make them visually distinct.
steps.hint: Add the <ul> element after your existing content. Inside it, create three <li> elements. Use the style attribute on each <li> with different CSS properties like backgroundColor, color, padding, or margin.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a styled list
  • First item
  • Second item
  • Third item
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now display a styled list with three items, each having distinct inline styles.
successCriteria: An unordered list (<ul>) is present in the return statement
Three list items (<li>) are inside the <ul>
Each <li> has a style attribute with inline CSS properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a styled list with inline styles on each item.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have an unordered list with three list items, each with inline styles applied via the style attribute.
steps.feedbackWrong: The list isn't quite right. Check that you have an unordered list (<ul>) containing three list items (<li>), each with inline styles.

steps.title: Export the component
steps.instruction: Add an export default statement for your App component so it can be imported and used in other files.
steps.hint: Place the export statement at the end of your file, after the component definition.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of exporting a component
export default MyComponent;
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is properly exported and ready to be imported elsewhere.
successCriteria: The file contains an export default statement
The exported value is the App component
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the App component. This makes it available for import in other files, completing your component setup.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using 'export default' followed by the component name (App).
steps.feedbackWrong: The export statement is missing or incorrect. Use 'export default App;' at the end of your file.
